title: Atoms, isotopes and energy levels
cards: A tiny nucleus, a much larger atom

An atom has a radius of about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Its positive nucleus contains protons and neutrons and holds most of its mass. The nuclear radius is less than one ten-thousandth of the atomic radius. The enlarged nucleus in this view cannot share the electron-shell scale.
Read the nuclear account

Atomic number Z counts protons. Mass number A counts protons plus neutrons; neutrons = A − Z. Neutral atoms have Z electrons. Isotopes share Z but differ in neutron number. A carbon-14 atom has 6 protons, 8 neutrons and 6 electrons. Losing an outer electron makes a positive ion without changing the nucleus.
Energy enters and leaves

Absorbing electromagnetic radiation can move an electron to a higher energy level, farther from the nucleus. A transition to a lower level emits electromagnetic radiation. These are electron transitions; they do not change proton number or describe nuclear decay.
Change the isotope or charge

Choose carbon-12 or carbon-14, then a neutral atom or singly positive ion. Predict the neutron and electron counts before revealing. Isotope changes affect neutrons; ion formation affects electrons. Shell rings and glowing markers are a teaching convention, not literal planetary paths.

title: How evidence changed the atom
cards: Models answer to evidence

The early indivisible-sphere model changed after the electron was discovered. The plum-pudding model placed negative electrons inside spread-out positive charge. A scientific model must explain observations and may be replaced when new evidence disagrees.
Most pass through; a few turn back

In alpha scattering, most particles passed through thin metal foil with little deflection: the atom is mostly empty space. A small fraction deflected strongly or returned: positive charge and much of the mass occupy a tiny dense nucleus. The movie deliberately shows rare large deflections more often so you can see them.
Refine the nuclear model

Bohr proposed electrons at specific distances/energy levels; his calculations agreed with observations. Later work identified proton units of positive nuclear charge. Chadwick supplied evidence for neutrons about twenty years after the nuclear model was accepted. Detailed Bohr and Chadwick experimental apparatus is not required.
Test an explanation

Compare spread-out positive charge with a concentrated nucleus. Choose a beam passing far from the centre or close to it. Predict the model’s qualitative deflection. Individual paths and encounter frequencies are schematic; use the actual distribution of observations, not this edited movie, as historical evidence.

title: Activity and types of radiation
cards: An unstable nucleus changes

Radioactive decay is spontaneous and random: you cannot predict exactly when one nucleus will decay. Activity counts decays per second, in becquerel (Bq). A detector’s count rate counts recorded events per second; geometry, absorption and detector efficiency mean it need not equal the source activity.
Three emissions, different identities

Alpha is a helium nucleus: two protons and two neutrons. Beta-minus is a fast electron produced in the nucleus when a neutron becomes a proton; it is not an electron falling out of an outer shell. Gamma is electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus. Neutron emission is also possible.
Penetration and ionisation

Alpha is strongly ionising with a short air range (a few centimetres) and is stopped by paper/skin. Beta has intermediate ionisation and range, and thin aluminium can stop it. Gamma is weakly ionising and very penetrating; thick lead or concrete reduces its intensity rather than guaranteeing zero transmission.
Match a source to a job

A thickness gauge needs some radiation absorbed and some transmitted. An external source must reach its target; an internal alpha emitter can be very damaging to nearby tissue. Compare alpha/beta through paper/aluminium. Our barrier model gives qualitative outcomes, not dose or exact shield thicknesses.

title: Balance nuclear equations
cards: Keep two accounts

Nuclear equations balance total mass number (top number A) and atomic number/charge number (bottom number Z) on each side. Use ⁴₂α and ⁰₋₁β for alpha and beta-minus. The daughter element symbol may be supplied; identifying an unfamiliar daughter element is not required.
Alpha removes a small nucleus

In single alpha decay, the daughter has A − 4 and Z − 2. A parent with A=210,Z=84 produces a daughter with A=206,Z=82 plus ⁴₂α. The whole equation still totals A=210 and Z=84. Mass number is a nucleon count, not the emitted energy.
Beta changes nuclear charge

In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton. Daughter A stays the same and Z increases by one; adding the emitted electron’s −1 balances charge. With A=14,Z=6, the daughter has A=14,Z=7. Gamma emission changes neither A nor Z.
Rebuild the ledger

Select one of two supplied parents and alpha/beta decay. Predict daughter A and Z before revealing. The animation isolates one event and uses enlarged symbols; it is not a prediction of a particular atom’s waiting time. Conservation applies to the entire equation, not the daughter alone.

title: Random decay and half-life
cards: Random individuals, predictable populations

A single nucleus has no scheduled decay time. For a large sample, a roughly constant fraction decays in equal intervals. Half-life is the time for the number of original unstable nuclei, activity or background-corrected count rate to fall to half its starting value.
Read a decay curve

For a source count rate 80,40,20,10 counts/s at 0,4,8,12 minutes, the half-life is 4 minutes. Start at any point and find the time to half that value. Equal half-lives remove equal fractions, not equal absolute counts. Small samples fluctuate more around a smooth expected curve.
Remove background first

If total rate is 50 counts/s and background is 10, the source contributes 40. Half this source rate is 20, so the corresponding total is 30, not 25. Keep detector geometry and counting time comparable; repeated/longer counts reduce relative random variation.
Follow an expected population

Choose 80 or 160 original nuclei and one or two half-lives. Predict the expected survivors. Markers disappear in a deterministic teaching sequence; real individual decay times are random. The smooth account gives an expectation, not a guarantee for a small real sample.

title: Contamination, irradiation and protection
cards: Source material or exposure?

Contamination means unwanted radioactive material is present on or inside something. It continues emitting until removed or decayed. Irradiation means exposure to nuclear radiation; ordinary irradiation in this GCSE model does not make the exposed object radioactive.
Follow what remains

Move a sealed source away and irradiation from it ends. Remove an external source but leave contaminating dust behind and that dust remains a source. Contamination can spread; external irradiation is not itself a transferable substance. Alpha’s short range is little protection when an alpha source is inside tissue.
Reduce unnecessary exposure

Use the shortest suitable exposure time, greater distance and appropriate shielding. Handle school sources only through supervised approved procedures, using suitable holders and secure storage. Containment reduces contamination; shielding reduces irradiation. The type of emission and exposure route affect risk.
Scrutinise claims

Studies about radiation effects should publish methods, results and limitations so other scientists can check them through peer review and further research. One result is not certainty. Compare sealed versus leaking sources and whether the source has been moved away; predict whether local radioactive material remains.

title: Background radiation and dose
cards: Radiation is already around us

Natural background includes radioactive rocks (including radon from the ground) and cosmic radiation. Human-made sources include fallout from nuclear tests and accidents. Location and occupation change exposure. A detector reading without an experimental source is not necessarily zero.
Compare dose with units

Radiation dose is expressed in sieverts (Sv); 1 Sv = 1000 mSv. You are not required to recall the unit, but must use supplied units consistently. Dose and health risk depend on exposure conditions; detector counts are not automatically a dose measurement.
Half-life is part of a risk account

For the same number of radioactive nuclei, shorter half-life means higher initial activity. Long-lived material remains an issue for longer. Compare activity, radiation type, amount, exposure route and duration; half-life alone cannot rank every hazard.
Correct a detector reading

Choose an illustrative site background and a measured total count rate. Subtract background to estimate source count rate, keeping geometry/time comparable. These invented counts demonstrate data correction; they are not local radiation surveys or personal dose estimates.

title: Using radiation in medicine
cards: Trace an organ’s function

A radioactive tracer can be introduced into the body and detected outside it. A suitable gamma emitter can provide a signal that escapes the body. Its half-life should allow the measurement but avoid unnecessary prolonged exposure; chemistry should target the intended pathway.
Treat unwanted tissue

Radiotherapy uses ionising radiation to damage or destroy unwanted tissue. External beams can be aimed from several directions to concentrate dose at the target while limiting healthy-tissue exposure. Some treatments use sources placed near or within the target. This is a conceptual comparison, not a treatment plan.
Weigh benefit and harm

Evaluate supplied evidence about diagnostic or treatment benefit alongside radiation harm, alternatives, uncertainty and consequences of doing nothing. A short half-life is not automatically suitable if most activity disappears before a tracer reaches the organ. A long half-life may prolong unnecessary exposure.
Choose for a stated purpose

Compare a tracer requiring external detection with a source intended to deposit energy close to tissue. Select a short-range strongly ionising alpha emission or penetrating gamma radiation and predict whether it matches the stated physical purpose. Real clinical selection needs many additional factors.

a: Deposit energy over a short distance

title: Nuclear fission and chain reactions
cards: Split a large unstable nucleus

Fission splits a large unstable nucleus, such as uranium or plutonium. Spontaneous fission is rare; usually the nucleus first absorbs a neutron. The split produces two smaller nuclei of roughly similar size, two or three neutrons and gamma radiation.
Track the released energy

The products have kinetic energy and energy is released. A chain reaction occurs when emitted neutrons trigger further fissions. Not every emitted neutron must cause another event: some escape or are absorbed without causing fission. Our diagram shows a selected branch, not exact reactor geometry.
Control the chain

A reactor controls the chain reaction and energy release, using neutron absorption to regulate further fissions. An uncontrolled chain reaction is associated with a nuclear weapon. Reactor operation and weapon engineering are not equivalent; the lesson models only the principle of neutron multiplication/control.
Count a toy generation

Choose one or two starting fissions and one or two successful next-generation triggers per fission. Predict next-generation fissions. Real products and neutron numbers vary; this branching arithmetic is an illustrative model, not a real reactor criticality calculation.

title: Nuclear fusion and energy
cards: Join light nuclei

Nuclear fusion joins two light nuclei into a heavier nucleus. In a fusion reaction, some mass can be converted into energy carried by radiation and other products. Fusion supplies energy in stars; it is distinct from chemical bonding and from fission of a heavy nucleus.
Overcome electric repulsion

Positive nuclei repel. Very high temperatures give nuclei enough kinetic energy for close encounters that can lead to fusion. Stellar conditions sustain fusion; this animation is a schematic successful event, not a collision probability model or a laboratory design.
Compare three changes

Fission splits a large nucleus; fusion joins light nuclei; a chemical reaction rearranges electrons and bonds without changing the nuclei. Neither fusion nor fission should be explained as ordinary burning. Products and released radiation carry the energy away.
Keep the nucleon ledger

For an illustrative hydrogen-2 plus hydrogen-3 reaction, helium-4 plus a neutron conserves total A=5 and Z=2. Choose repeated copies of this supplied reaction and predict total nucleon count before the reaction. The mass difference involves binding energy; integer mass numbers count nucleons and do not measure exact rest masses.
